title: 800 Fed At Savoy Barbecue; Fire Truck Fund Nets $900
text:
800 Fed At Savoy Barbecue; Fire Truck Fund Nets $900

SAVOY— There was about enough barbecue left over to feed the volunteer workers but the two dozen or more who had put in four hours dishing it out couldn't look a baked bean or a hunk of barbecue in the eye.

But the important thing was that $900 was added to the swelling Savoy fire truck fund by the barbecue. The affair was sponsored by the truckless volunteer firemen.

Mrs. Davis headed up the food committee. She went to the other cities and got contributions. She asked Mrs. Minnie Springfield and Mrs. James Burris from the Baptists, Mrs. Elbert Hutchins and Mrs. Tom Lane from the Church of Christ and she selected Miss Thelma Jo Lane, Mrs. Max Artery and Mrs. Gene Lawrence. Collins, communities in Fanin County became centers for private accommodation for the more advanced subjects such as Latin, Greek, philosophy and geography were taught compulsory were strictly enforced. Carlton College in Bonham and the Savoy Male College were the best of the district's two leading colleges in the area.

She asked the women to enlist the aid of as many women as necessary to come up with enough potato salad and other trimmings to feed 800 people. Mrs. Davis figured 75 women making five pounds each of potato salad should feed about 100 cakes would fill the bill.

There is no more than 100 families in Savoy, but the 800 who dip into the community for miles in all directions.

No one brought as little as five-pounds of potato salad, most brought from six to 16 pounds. There were 100 cakes on hand when the doors opened and another 25 to 30 or two arrived during the evening.

Mrs. Davis got the tea and coffee going. The drinks and dressings from Kraft, the milk from Borden's and the margarine from Blue Bonnet. Five bread companies—Mrs. Baird's, Pinneys, Holsom, Wonder and Rainbo—contributed the bread. D. Peplar Bargs and Mission orange were furnished free, too.

The Bells Methodist Church and the Marvin Methodists north of Bonham to augment the hundreds of large coffee urns. Dishes came from the Bells school to augment the donation table and service, two large floor fans, four pews, the pulpit stand and two chairs.

Glenn McKinney and Thomas Strickland smoked 800 pounds of boned beef on to barbecue at 7 p.m. Thursday and 22 hours later, cooked it to flavor, not necessarily on wood, the first serving was dished out to Elmore Proctor of Savoy.

A steady stream of people from all neighboring towns poured into Savoy from 3 to 11 p.m. to peer over a wash tub saying "let's do-nate" to the fire truck fund. The sign "buy a fire truck" brought smiles to the faces of well-fed citizens and visitors from their pocketbooks.

General chairman Claude Strickland said the tub added "at least $900" to the total.

There were 600 tickets sold in advance and another 200 bought at the door. That total plus the tub money brought in a little more than $2,700. Total expenses were only $120, with Strickland confident that the "final figure will show a net profit of $2,700."

"That puts about $1,300 into our fire truck fund," he said, since the truck itself would cost $4,000. We're confident of getting the truck—maybe it's fish frys, chili suppers and things of that nature held. We're going to get our fire truck. We'll get it without a bond issue."

Bakers of the Friday night feed had only praise for all who helped. But with $2,700 still needed, they were planning their organizational move next move to congratulate themselves on the success of their initial venture.
notes: Text in the middle section has some apparent scrambling/corruption — a passage about Carlton College in Bonham and Savoy Male College appears to be an insertion from a different document, possibly mis-scanned. Transcribed verbatim as it appears.
